1.	Resolved, that the general officer commending the militia shall he paid at the rate of $6,000 per annum ; the adjutant-general, at the rate of $3,200 per annum , and the quartermaster general, at the rate of $3,200 per annum.
2.	Resolved, that the permanent force shall be entitled to daily pay and allowances at the rates prescribed by the Governor in Council , and that the pay of privates shall not exceed 75'cents a day, and of buglers under 18 years of age 40 cents a day.
3.	Resolved, that officers, warrant officers, and non-commissioned officers of the active militia, other than the permanent force, shall be entitled to pay at rates prescribed by the Governor in Council ; and that the jiay of privates therein shall be at the rate o'f 60 cents a day on appointment, which may be increased to a maximum of $1 a day during the third year of service.
4.	Resolved, that an allowance of one dollar per diem, or such other rate as may be prescribed, will be paid to each officer and man for every horse actually and necessarily used by him, when on active service, during a period of annual drill and training, or when otherwise on duty as aforesaid.

As these are the resolutions on which the Bill now before the House is based, I thought it would be convenient to have them put through the committee before we again take up the consideration of the Bill. In the first resolution, as a result of the discussion which took place the other night, I want to make a slight change. I want to add the following words : ' and the director general of ordnance, at the rate of $3,200 per annum.' At the time the present law was passed the stores were in the hands of the civil side of the Militia Department. The ordnance branch is now on the military side of the department, and is one of the important divisions, and the rate of pay is the same as that officer is receiving now. I hope the committee will allow this change to be made.
Tbe change will require the assent of His Excellency, I presume ?
I have His Excellency's assent.
Tbe announcement should be made with tbe Speaker in tbe chair. It is not a matter of very much moment, but we should proceed regularly.

Forty cents a day is the pay of the men. The pay of the non-commissioned officers differs ; but that is not affected by this resolution. It is left to be fixed by the Governor in Council.

I explained, on introducing the Bill, that we intended to adopt, by regulation, the system of the Northwest Mounted Police, which is this : On enlistment he will receive fifty cents a day and five cents per day additional each year until it reaches seventy-five cents per day.

The hon. minister will be good enough to remember that-I was fair enough to give him absolute credit for increasing the salary up to the present standard. But now the matter has ueen brought up, he will be fair enough to admit that I drew his attention to the matter long ago. When I was in Australia I found that the little colony of New South Wales ]>aid its general officer commanding more than we pay for the whole Dominion. The minister will also note that every officer in the departments, when he travels on the business of the country, lias his expenses paid. We have only to turn up the Auditor General's Report to find that thousands of dollars are paid out for the travelling expenses of ministers, ministers' secretaries and other officers. Therefore, it cannot be regarded as a concession to the general officer commanding that, when he travels from place to place in the execution of the duties of his office, his expenses are paid. In that respect he receives only what every other officer receives. 1 Now, the officer in command in Scotland, who has only 9,000 troops under him-as against some 40,000 or 50,000 in Canada-receives $13,000 a year. All these figures that I have given can be found in the Statesman's Year-book.
Would not that be 9,000 regulars? In addition there are the militia.

About five regiments of militia and volunteers. I have had the privilege of seeing every one of them on parade. We do not ask that the general officer commanding here should be paid any such salary as the officer in command in Scotland. But, let us hope that when the minister brings his measure down we shall find that that clause Is eliminated which intimates that this increased salary is' in lieu of other allowances, so that the general officer commanding may find that expenses that are forced upon him by reason of his position will be borne by the nation. I think that is fair.

May I ask the minister if this sum of $6,000 per annum and expenses to which lie has made reference covers the total obligation to be imposed on the country by the appointment of such an officer? For instance, when his term expires does he receive any pension or allowance, such as half pay?

Not from Canada. If lie is an imperial officer he returns to his service in the imperial army. If it should turn out that a Canadian is appointed, as will be possible under tlie Bill if it becomes law, then, of course, lie would he provided for by Canada. He will, no doubt, be a member of the permanent



force of the militia for which a Pension Law was provided by parliament three or four years ago, and will be pensioned under the provisions of that law. Or, possibly-wliat I think is much more likely to happen, it he were a young man and a good man-by a system of exchange which is now under consideration as between the War Office and the government of this country, he might be given a position on the staff, or some other important position in the British service, if he wished it.
Does not the general officer commanding draw his pay as an officer of the imperial army while he holds this position ?
No, I think not.
I think he does.
Then, there is some scheme in contemplation whereby Canadian officers occupying superior positions in the active militia shall be transferred, under certain terms to the imperial service?
That might be done ; I do not say it will be done.

I understood the minister to suggest that if it should happen that a Canadian were appointed as general officer commanding, if he were a young active man, he might be sent to obtain further military knowledge in connection with the imperial forces.

I will explain further. At present, we give to imperial officers a number of positions in this country. The commandant of the Royal Military College and, I think, at least four professors of that college are officers drawn from the imperial army. We at present draw our general officer commanding from that army. It has been the custom frequently to appoint to the position of quartermaster general an imperial officer. And, at this moment the position of chief intelligence officer of this country is held by an imperial officer. It has been pointed out to the imperial authorities that it would be a fair thing to them to give to Canadians who are qualified the same number of positions, or a certain number of positions temporarily in the British army. That question is being considered, and I think it very likely that some arrangement will be reached.

I do not so regard it. Tbe statute reads as follows : ' There shall be appointed an officer holding the rank of colonel or rank superior thereto in Her Majesty's regular army.' That does not discriminate against any Canadian. It simply requires that any man appointed, be he Australian, Canadian or British, shall have a certain experience, It would be a perfectly good argument if my hon. friend would argue, as he has not yet done, that Canadian officers have now the experience which is equivalent to that gained by er officer in the regular army of Great Britain. That is an argument I have not yet heard, and to which I shall give due consideration when it is made, but in the meantime there is no more discrimination in this case than there is against a lawyer who has not served ten years at the bar, and who, however able he may be, he cannot be appointed a judge on account of his not having the requisite experience. Does not the provision my hon. friend proposes discriminate against the officers of the Northwest Mounted Police ? Are there not in that corps able and efficient officers ? My hon. friend says the law now discriminates against the militia of Canada. It is no more a discrimination against the militia of Canada than against the nili-tia of Great Britain or Australia or any other country. The case'he brings up about the appointment to the Supreme Court of Canada is not an analogous one, because a man who has served ten or fifteen years at the bar of this country has necessarily all the experience required to make him competent to fill the position of chief justice. But is there not a distinction between service in the militia and service in the regular army ? If you can show that the service of an officer in the Canadian militia gives him substantially as good an experience as service in the regular army of Great Britain, then it goes without saying that the measure which the hon. gentleman is introducing ought to be carried. There should not be any discrimination against Canadians, and I do not regard the present law as discrimination of that kind, but as providing that a certain experience on the part of any man, be he a Canadian, British or Australian officer, shall be necessary before he can fill the position of general officer commanding in this country.

I think that my hon. friend the leader bf the opposition, in advancing the argument that the militia of England and Canada are in the same category, is labouring under a mistake. We have in Canada in reality a regular army, small though it may be. But we still call them the militia. We do not distinguish, between our permanent and non-permanent force by calling one the regular army and the other the militia. In England the direct contrary is the case. To permit an officer of the militia in England to assume

a high command would be to open the door to the appointment of men of inexperience,
I admit. And it may be that here in Canada the door is open to the appointment of inexperience. But, at the same time we have available in the militia-in the permanent part thereof-men whose experience is probably as good, and in the future, it will be as good, as that of the officers of any regiment in the regular army at home. That being the case, I really fail to see why we should not give the highest appointment in the gift of the government in military matters to a Canadian, if he he fit for it. And, if he be not fit for it, let us hold the government responsible. What is the meaning of responsible government if that be not it ? Why this government could accept as comAafider of our forces some gentleman from the English regular army utterly incompetent for the post

for there are some incompetents there ; without wishing to cast slurs upon the service we can say that that is undoubtedly the case. Where, then, is the danger in opening this office when wre can hold the government responsible ? It has been urged by some gentlemen on the opposition side that this is severing another link with the mother country. I fail to see that. I recall the lessons of history and I remember that, about a hundred and twenty-five years ago, the thirteen colonies broke away from the motherland, and some historians of undoubted authority say that it was more the way British gentlemen treated colonial gentlemen that caused that severance than any question of the duty on tea. If we are to continue our close connection with the motherland, it must be on terms of equality. That is the only thing you can ask worthy sons of worthy sires to stand for, and it' is the only thing that Canadians are ready to admit. It is not a reflection on British officers that this change should be made, but it is undoubtedly an acknowledgment of ability and fitness on the part of Canadians.

Under these circumstances, the House might reasonably have expected the hon. gentleman to have come back and asked for a new vote under the new conditions that had arisen. I do not know a greater evil in a great spending department, where the temptation to over-expend is very great.
